analogy.p: Imagine a restaurant that became famous for one star dish (oil). Business booms, but when the price of ingredients or customer demand for that dish falls, the whole restaurant suffers; the owners (TNCs and the elite) take most of the profit; and the kitchen's smoke and spills affect the neighbours (the Niger Delta). Improving the menu with new dishes (diversification: manufacturing, telecoms, services) and sharing the profit more fairly would make the restaurant stronger. The analogy breaks down because Nigeria is a huge, varied country of over 200 million people, not one business, and its challenges also include politics, security and regional inequality.
analogy.t: Nigeria's economy as a restaurant with one star dish

bullets: Classified as a **newly emerging economy (NEE)** by many courses, although it still has features of an LIC (high poverty, low HDI); say which classification your course uses and why.
**Regional importance**: member of the **African Union** and **ECOWAS** (Economic Community of West African States); a leading peacekeeping and political voice in West Africa.
**Global importance**: a member of **OPEC** and a major oil producer and exporter; member of the **Commonwealth** and the **UN**; large market of over 200 million consumers attracting TNCs.
**Large population**: one of the world's most populous countries, with a young population and fast population growth.
Former British colony, independent since **1960**; English is the official language, which helps trade and links with the UK.
Cities: **Lagos** (a megacity), **Abuja**, **Kano** in the north and **Port Harcourt** in the oil-producing Niger Delta.
Remember to give **place-specific facts** (names of cities, regions, companies) in case-study answers; marks are lost for vague points.
core.p: Nigeria is a country in **West Africa**, on the coast of the **Gulf of Guinea** (part of the Atlantic Ocean). It borders **Benin** to the west, **Niger** to the north, **Chad** to the north-east and **Cameroon** to the east. Its capital is **Abuja**, built near the centre of the country and made the capital in 1991 in place of Lagos, while **Lagos** remains the largest city and main commercial centre. Nigeria is the **most populous country in Africa** (over 200 million people) and one of the continent's largest economies, so it matters both regionally (as a leader in West Africa) and globally (as a major oil producer).

bullets: **Languages**: English is the official language; Hausa, Yoruba and Igbo are widely spoken, among hundreds of others.
**Religion**: Islam is more common in the north, Christianity in the south; religious tensions have contributed to conflict in some areas.

**Culture**: **Nollywood** is one of the world's biggest film industries by number of films; Nigerian music (Afrobeats) and literature have global influence, boosting the country's international image and creating jobs.
**Young population**: a large proportion are under 25, so demand for education and jobs is high; unemployment and underemployment are major problems.
**Urbanisation**: millions have migrated to cities such as Lagos looking for jobs, causing growth of **slums/informal settlements** with poor sanitation.
**Inequality**: wealth is concentrated in cities and among the elite, while poverty is higher in the rural north and the Niger Delta communities.
Use this to explain how cultural diversity can be both an asset (a diverse economy and culture) and a challenge (conflicts and uneven development).
core.p: Nigeria is extremely diverse, with more than **250 ethnic groups** and hundreds of languages. The largest groups are the **Hausa-Fulani** in the north, the **Yoruba** in the south-west and the **Igbo** in the south-east. The north is predominantly **Muslim** and the south predominantly **Christian**, with many people following traditional beliefs too. This diversity is a source of cultural strength, shown by music (Afrobeats) and the film industry **Nollywood**, but it can also create tensions and political competition. Nigeria's young and rapidly growing population creates a large workforce and market but puts pressure on schools, jobs, housing and health services.

bullets: **Political**: federal republic; return to democracy in 1999; **corruption** and political instability reduce the effectiveness of development projects and deter some investors.
**Security**: conflict and insurgency in the north-east and tensions in the Niger Delta have displaced people and harmed the economy.
**Climate**: tropical in the south (wet, forested, high rainfall) and drier in the north; the north is vulnerable to **drought and desertification**.
**Niger Delta**: one of the world's largest wetlands, with rich biodiversity (mangroves, fisheries) but heavily affected by oil extraction.
**Resources**: large reserves of **oil and natural gas**; also coal, tin and limestone, and fertile land for crops such as cassava, yams, cocoa and palm oil.
**Infrastructure** problems: unreliable electricity supply (many businesses use diesel generators), poor roads and congested ports increase costs.
Political stability and good governance are important for development: link to the **causes of uneven development** (conflict, corruption).
core.p: Nigeria is a **federal republic** made up of 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory. After independence it experienced periods of military rule, and a return to **democratic civilian government in 1999**. Corruption, weak institutions and security problems, including insurgency in the north-east, are challenges that discourage investment and slow development. Environmentally, Nigeria has varied landscapes: mangrove swamps and rainforest on the coast and in the **Niger Delta**, savanna in the middle belt, and semi-arid **Sahel** in the north where **desertification** and the shrinking of Lake Chad threaten farming.

bullets: **Primary**: agriculture still employs a large share of people, but is often small-scale subsistence farming with low productivity; oil and gas extraction dominates exports.
**Secondary**: growth of manufacturing such as cement, food and beverages, and the large **Dangote refinery** near Lagos, which aims to reduce dependence on imported fuel.
**Tertiary**: growth of **telecoms (mobile phones), banking/fintech, retail, Nollywood and tourism**; Lagos is a hub for technology start-ups.
**Quaternary**: growing ICT and technology sector in Lagos.
**Structural change** follows the Clark-Fisher pattern: from primary towards secondary and tertiary as the economy develops.
**Oil dependence** makes the economy unstable: government income and the value of the currency fall when oil prices fall, making it vulnerable.
Industrial growth is concentrated in **Lagos and a few cities**, so there is a regional development gap between south and north.
core.p: At independence in 1960 most Nigerians worked in **agriculture** and the main exports were cash crops such as **cocoa, groundnuts and palm oil**. After oil was discovered in commercial quantities at **Oloibiri in 1956**, oil production grew rapidly, especially in the 1970s, and **crude oil became the dominant export**, providing the majority of export earnings and a large share of government revenue. Since then, governments have tried to **diversify** the economy because dependence on oil leaves Nigeria vulnerable to falling world oil prices. The **secondary sector** (e.g. cement, food and drink, textiles, and refining) and the **tertiary sector** (telecommunications, banking, retail, film and ICT) have grown, and the **service sector** now makes up the largest share of GDP.

bullets: **Benefits**: jobs (direct and indirect), taxes and royalties for government, infrastructure such as roads and power built for operations, skills and technology transfer, export earnings.
**Multiplier effect**: wages spent locally and use of local suppliers create further jobs in construction, catering and transport.
**Costs**: profits **repatriated** (leakage); oil industry is capital-intensive so creates relatively few jobs for the amount of money earned (an **enclave economy**).
**Environmental costs**: oil spills, **gas flaring** and habitat loss in the Niger Delta; clean-up has been slow and disputed.
**Social costs**: pollution damages farming and fishing, which many local people rely on; conflict and protests, e.g. in Ogoniland, have occurred over benefits and damage.
**Political power**: large TNCs can have great influence over government decisions and may avoid tax.
Use a balanced judgement: TNCs have helped Nigeria's economy grow, but benefits have not been shared equally and the environmental costs have been high.
core.h: Role of TNCs in Nigeria's economy
core.p: Transnational corporations are central to Nigeria's economy. The oil industry is dominated by TNCs such as **Shell, Chevron, ExxonMobil, TotalEnergies and Eni**, often working in joint ventures with the state-owned oil company. Other TNCs operate in telecoms (e.g. MTN), food and drink and consumer goods (e.g. Unilever, Nestlé, Coca-Cola). TNCs bring **investment, jobs, taxes and royalties, technology and export earnings**, and the multiplier effect creates more jobs in supply industries and services. However, much of the profit is sent abroad, many jobs go to foreign specialists, and oil extraction has caused serious pollution in the Niger Delta.

bullets: **Historical links**: British colony, then independence in 1960; Commonwealth membership; strong cultural and trading ties with the UK.
**OPEC membership** gives Nigeria a say in global oil production and prices.
**Exports**: mainly crude oil and gas; other exports include cocoa and other agricultural products. **Imports**: machinery, manufactured goods, food and refined fuel.
**New partners**: China has invested in infrastructure and trade; India is a major buyer of Nigerian oil.
**Regional trade**: ECOWAS aims to improve trade and free movement among West African states; the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) also aims to boost trade within Africa.
Increased trade and investment bring growth but risks of **debt** and **dependence on one commodity**.
Link to the **development gap** strategies: trade, investment and aid all connect Nigeria to the global economy.
core.p: Nigeria's relationships with the wider world have changed since independence. It was part of the British Empire until 1960 and still has strong links through the **Commonwealth**, the English language and trade with the UK. Since the 1970s its membership of **OPEC** and its oil exports have connected it to markets in Europe, Asia and the Americas. In more recent decades **China and India** have become more important trading partners and investors, for example **Chinese investment in railways, ports and infrastructure**, while the UK and EU remain important. Regionally, Nigeria plays a leading role in **ECOWAS** and the **African Union**, promoting trade and security in Africa.

bullets: **Types**: bilateral (e.g. UK government programmes), multilateral (World Bank, UN) and voluntary (NGOs and charities); emergency aid to conflict-affected areas in the north-east.
**Benefits**: improved health (vaccination, e.g. polio), education, water supply and support for women and farmers; emergency food and shelter for displaced people.
**Drawbacks**: corruption can divert money; some aid is **tied** to donors' companies; projects may not be sustainable once funding ends; risk of dependency.
**Debt**: Nigeria received **debt relief** in 2005 when a large part of its external debt to the Paris Club was cancelled, freeing money for development.
Aid is a **top-down** strategy when it is large government-to-government schemes and **bottom-up** when delivered via NGOs and local communities.
Judge effectiveness by evidence: did health, education and income improve and did benefits reach the poorest?
Link to **Fairtrade, microfinance and intermediate technology** projects run by NGOs in rural Nigeria.
core.p: Nigeria receives **international aid** from governments (bilateral aid from countries such as the UK, USA and Japan), from international organisations (multilateral aid such as the World Bank, UN agencies and the EU) and from charities (voluntary aid such as the Gates Foundation, Oxfam and Save the Children). Aid has funded health programmes, education, water, sanitation and emergency relief. A major success was the campaign against polio: with support from WHO, UNICEF and charities, Nigeria was declared free of the wild poliovirus in 2020, and Africa was certified wild-polio-free. However, because Nigeria is a large oil-producing economy, aid is small compared with its population and economy, and critics point to corruption and dependency.

bullets: **Positive**: rising incomes for some, expansion of mobile phone and internet use, growth of the service sector and entrepreneurship, improvements in health such as vaccination programmes.
**Negative**: persistent **poverty and inequality**; high unemployment among young people; rapid urban growth with **slums**, congestion and pollution in Lagos.

**Health and education**: HDI is still in the low-to-medium range, life expectancy is low compared with HICs, and many children are out of school, especially in the north (check up-to-date figures in your textbook).
**Regional inequality**: the south-west (Lagos) is much richer than the north; the oil-producing Niger Delta has seen wealth leave while local people suffer pollution.
**Environmental quality**: oil spills, gas flaring, deforestation, air pollution and waste problems in cities.
**Measuring**: use indicators such as GNI per capita, HDI, life expectancy, literacy and access to safe water and electricity.
Evaluation: economic development has improved some aspects of life but has not yet reduced poverty enough or protected the environment.
core.h: Effects of development on quality of life
core.p: Economic growth has brought some benefits to Nigeria's people: more jobs in services and industry, a growing middle class in cities such as Lagos, improved mobile phone and internet access, and better health and education than in the past. However, benefits are **unequally shared**. A large proportion of the population still lives in poverty (about two-fifths below the national poverty line in recent surveys), life expectancy and literacy remain lower than in HICs, and many people lack reliable electricity, clean water and sanitation. The north and rural areas lag behind the south and cities, and rapid urban growth has created slums.

bullets: **Niger Delta oil spills** damage mangrove forests and fishing grounds, so local incomes fall and drinking water is polluted.
**Gas flaring** wastes energy, releases CO2 and soot, and affects health and farmland near flares.
**Ogoniland** is a well-known example where pollution and conflict with oil companies led to protests; clean-up programmes have been slow.
**Urban**: Lagos faces air pollution, traffic congestion, poor waste disposal and flooding.
**Deforestation and desertification** reduce soil quality and farming productivity, especially in the north.
**Possible management**: stricter regulation and fines, improving pipeline maintenance, ending gas flaring, clean-up and compensation, renewable energy and sustainable farming.
Link to **sustainable development**: economic growth that damages the environment and local livelihoods is not sustainable.
core.p: Economic development in Nigeria has had significant environmental costs. Oil extraction in the **Niger Delta** has caused thousands of oil spills from leaking pipelines, accidents, theft and sabotage, which pollute land, creeks and groundwater, kill fish and destroy **mangroves**. **Gas flaring** (burning off gas released during oil extraction) releases carbon dioxide and other pollutants and contributes to climate change and acid rain. Elsewhere, rapid urban growth causes air and water pollution and waste problems, while deforestation for farming, fuelwood and timber and desertification in the north reduce biodiversity and farmland.

bullets: **Strengths**: large population and market, oil and gas reserves, diversifying economy, strong cultural industries, regional leadership.
**Weaknesses**: dependence on oil, corruption, unreliable electricity, regional inequality, security problems, pollution.
**Opportunities**: growth of services, technology, agriculture, regional trade (ECOWAS, AfCFTA) and renewable energy.
**Threats**: falling oil prices, climate change (desertification, flooding), population pressure, political instability.
Judgement structure: 'Development has improved ... for ..., but ... remains ... because ...'.
Always use **place-specific** names: Lagos, Abuja, Niger Delta, Ogoniland, Shell, Dangote, Nollywood, ECOWAS, OPEC.
Check which case study your teacher has used (Nigeria is a common choice for an NEE or LIC); adapt the details to your own course notes.
core.p: Nigeria shows both the potential and the problems of an emerging economy. It has size, natural resources, a young population, a diversifying economy and cultural influence. Yet oil dependence, corruption, inequality, poor infrastructure, insecurity and environmental damage have held back development, and the benefits of growth have not reached many of the poorest. For an exam evaluation, you should be able to weigh these points, use specific facts, and reach a supported judgement about whether economic development has improved life for most Nigerians.

bullets: For 'location and importance' questions: use compass directions, neighbours, capital/major cities and regional/global roles (ECOWAS, OPEC, largest population in Africa).
For 'changing industrial structure': describe a shift (e.g. agriculture to oil to services) with approximate dates and examples, then say why it matters.
For 'TNCs': give two benefits and two costs, with named TNCs (Shell, MTN) and the multiplier and leakage ideas.
For 'aid': name types (bilateral, multilateral, voluntary), give an example (polio campaign) and one problem (corruption, dependency).
For 'quality of life and environment': give at least one positive and one negative for each, with evidence (Lagos slums, Niger Delta spills).
Use the data given: when a resource such as a graph or table is provided, always quote from it before adding case-study knowledge.
Keep figures approximate and state them as 'about' unless you have checked them, as figures change over time.
core.h: How to use the case study in exams
core.p: Case-study marks are awarded for accurate, specific, relevant information and for applying it to the question. You are never just 'telling the story' of Nigeria; you must answer the command word and the focus of the question (for example, the role of TNCs, aid, or the effects on quality of life and the environment). Choose three or four of your strongest facts, name the place or company, and explain what difference it makes. Practise structuring paragraphs using point, evidence, explanation and link back to the question.

exam: Typical question types: 'Describe the location and importance of your case study country' (4), 'Explain how TNCs affect the economy' (4), 'Assess the effects of economic development on quality of life and the environment' (6 + SPaG), and data-based questions on employment, GDP or trade.

**Describe**: give specific facts (location, neighbours, capital, regional role, population); **Explain**: link a fact to an effect using 'because' or 'which leads to'; **Assess**: weigh positives and negatives and reach a judgement.
Use **place-specific detail** to access top marks: Lagos, Abuja, Niger Delta, Ogoniland, Shell, MTN, Dangote refinery, Nollywood, ECOWAS, OPEC.
For 2-mark questions: a point plus a development, e.g. 'Oil is Nigeria's main export (1), so the economy is vulnerable when oil prices fall (1)'.
For 4-mark TNC questions: two developed points, e.g. benefit with the multiplier effect, and cost with leakage or oil spills.

For 6-mark questions: structure with a short intro, two or three developed paragraphs (benefits and costs or short term/long term), and a conclusion with a justified judgement; link back to the question each time.
For data questions: describe patterns using numbers and units, calculate changes (percentage change = change ÷ original × 100), and compare sectors or time periods.
Use **connectives** that show evaluation: 'however', 'on the other hand', 'overall', 'this is because', 'as a result'.
Avoid vague statements such as 'it helps the economy'; say how: jobs, taxes, exports, improved infrastructure.
Make sure the facts match the question; keep approximate figures as 'about', and only use facts you are certain are correct.

mistakes.r: Nigeria has a large, diversifying economy with oil, manufacturing and a fast-growing service sector (telecoms, Nollywood, banking); but it still has high poverty and inequality.
mistakes.w: Nigeria is a poor country with no industry.

mistakes.r: Give a balanced view: jobs, taxes, technology and the multiplier effect against leakage, pollution and few jobs per pound earned.
mistakes.w: TNCs only help Nigeria / TNCs only harm Nigeria.

mistakes.r: Abuja is the capital (since 1991); Lagos is the largest city and main commercial centre.
mistakes.w: Abuja is the biggest city and capital because it is the richest.

mistakes.r: Aid has helped with health (e.g. polio) and emergencies, but it is limited, can be lost to corruption and does not by itself create sustainable development.
Agriculture employs many people, but oil dominates exports; the economy is diversifying into manufacturing and services.
mistakes.w: Nigeria's economy depends on farming only.

mistakes.r: Select facts relevant to the question and use them to answer the command word, with place-specific evidence.
mistakes.w: The case study answer should describe everything about Nigeria.

mistakes.r: Benefits are unequal: wealth is concentrated in cities and among the elite, while Niger Delta communities suffer pollution.
mistakes.w: Oil money has been shared equally among Nigerians.

mistakes.r: It can improve incomes and services but also cause inequality, slums and pollution; evaluate both.
mistakes.w: Economic development always improves quality of life.

summary: This point is the AQA case study of one LIC or NEE, here Nigeria: its location and importance, social, political, cultural and environmental context, changing industrial structure, role of TNCs, changing trade and political relationships, international aid, and effects of economic development on quality of life and the environment. You must use accurate, place-specific facts to answer the command word, and it matters because case-study questions carry high marks on Paper 2.

terms.d: Newly emerging economy: a country that has begun to experience high rates of economic development, usually with rapid industrial growth.
Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries: a group of oil-producing countries that coordinate oil production and prices; Nigeria is a member.
Economic Community of West African States, a regional organisation promoting trade, cooperation and security among West African countries.
An association of mostly former British colonies, including Nigeria, with historic and cultural links.
The low-lying wetland region on Nigeria's south coast where the River Niger meets the sea; the main oil-producing region.
A change in the importance of the primary, secondary and tertiary sectors in an economy over time.
Developing a wider range of economic activities so an economy depends less on one product such as oil.
Transnational corporation: a company operating in several countries, such as Shell or MTN.
Sending profits earned in a country back to the company's home country.
The knock-on effect where money spent creates further jobs, income and demand in an economy.
Burning off unwanted natural gas released during oil extraction, causing air pollution and greenhouse gas emissions.
An industry, such as oil, that earns large sums but has few links with the rest of the economy and provides few local jobs.
Aid given directly from one government to another.
Aid given via international organisations such as the World Bank or the UN.
Aid given by charities and non-governmental organisations (NGOs) using public donations.
Human Development Index: a measure combining life expectancy, education and income per person.
Unplanned housing built by migrants, often without proper sanitation, electricity or legal ownership (slum).
The process by which fertile land becomes desert, usually through drought and unsustainable land use.

worked.ans: (a) 30 percentage points; (b) about 46 per cent; (c) the economy has developed with growth of secondary and tertiary jobs, so fewer people work in farming (Clark-Fisher structural change).
worked.q: The table (illustrative figures) shows the percentage of workers in the primary sector: 1970 = 65 per cent, 2020 = 35 per cent. Calculate (a) the change in percentage points and (b) the percentage decrease. Suggest one reason for the change. (4 marks)
steps: (b) Percentage decrease = (30 ÷ 65) × 100 = 46.15... = 46 per cent (nearest whole number).
(c) Reason: workers moved to secondary and tertiary jobs such as oil, manufacturing, telecoms and services in cities such as Lagos as the economy developed.

worked.q: A country has a GDP of US$440 billion (illustrative) and a population of 220 million. (a) Calculate GDP per person. (b) The population grows by 2.5 per cent in a year. Calculate how many extra people there are after one year. (3 marks)

worked.ans: In Nigeria, TNCs such as Shell and Chevron have helped the economy because they invest in oil extraction, which gives export earnings and tax and royalty income for the government, and provide jobs and infrastructure, creating a multiplier effect as workers spend wages locally. Telecoms firms such as MTN have also created jobs and improved communication. However, much of the profit is sent abroad (repatriated), and oil is an enclave industry that employs relatively few people, so the benefits have not been shared equally and the economy depends on oil prices. Environmentally, oil spills and gas flaring in the Niger Delta have polluted land and water, destroyed mangroves and harmed fishing and farming, so local people have lost their incomes. Overall, TNCs have boosted Nigeria's economy and government income, but the costs for the environment and local people mean the benefits are limited unless there is stronger regulation, clean-up and fairer sharing of the money.
worked.q: Using a case study of an LIC or NEE, assess the effects of TNCs on the country's economy and environment. (6 marks)
steps: Name the case study and TNCs: Nigeria; Shell, Chevron (oil), MTN (telecoms).
Developed economic benefits: jobs, taxes and royalties, export earnings, infrastructure, multiplier effect.
Developed economic costs: profits repatriated; oil is an enclave economy with few jobs; vulnerability to falling oil prices.
Environmental costs: oil spills and gas flaring in the Niger Delta, mangrove loss, polluted water and farmland.
Judgement with reasons: benefits for economy and government but unequal and harmful to local people unless regulated.
